3016.prule: No word-level stress rule stated. 3017.dloc: Vol. 1, III.8 'L'Accent', pp. 153-154; accent-as-length II.4.3 pp. 51-52; rules 19.1-26.2 pp. 154-162; tempo rules pp. 162-163; tonemes II.13.1 pp. 102-103
3017.prule: A structural (demarcative) accent, realised as vowel length, is assigned to every stem and root: it falls on the syllable immediately following the theme/radical boundary, i.e. the stem-initial syllable of nouns, verbs and pronominals, whatever the number of prefixes; trisyllabic CVCVNCV noun stems accent their second (= penultimate) syllable instead. No final vowel and no monosyllabic word is ever accented: a word-final monosyllabic stem retracts its accent onto the preceding prefix (rule 19.1) and an accent left before a word/phrase boundary is deleted (rule 24). Position is thus fixed relative to the stem boundary (morphological), not counted from the word edge and not weight-based.
3017.srule: Secondary accent (realised, like the main accent, as vowel length): a non-final syllable separated by one syllable from an accented syllable acquires an accent (rules 21.1, 21.2), giving a secondary accent two syllables to the right of the structural accent in words of five or more syllables with second-syllable accent (more rarely four-syllable words with initial accent); a VNC syllable before final -V (e.g. durative -àng-) also acquires a secondary accent wherever the structural accent is (rule 19.2); the first of two adjacent accents is deleted (rule 26.2); never on a final syllable.

3017.tone: Two contrastive lexical tonemes: 'Le tonème a une fonction distinctive.... Il y a deux tonèmes en gisira. Le tonème haut, noté /´/ ou H, et le tonème bas, noté /`/ ou B.' (pp. 102-103); HB and BH sequences on one vowel give contour tones; low tone lowered before # is an allophone. The accent is a separate, non-contrastive demarcative system whose exponent is vowel length (not pitch); the author notes few Bantu descriptions with a full tone system have used the notion of accent (p. 51-52).

tn.quote: Les tonèmes sont portés par les voyelles. Il y a deux tonèmes en glslra. Le tonème haut, noté /"/ ou H, et le tonème bas, noté /V ou B. Il s'agit de "tonèmes ponctuels" puisque leur hauteur mélodique reste invariable durant toute l'énonciation du phonème vocalique.qui les porte. Le signes / et / '^ / notent respectivement la combinaison des tonèmes H + B et B + H que porte un phonème vocalique. Ces combinaisons sont réalisées par un "ton modulé" puisqu'il y a variation de la hauteur mélodique au cours de l'émission du phonème vocalique.
tn.translation: Tonemes are carried by the vowels. There are two tonemes in Gisira: the high toneme, written /´/ or H, and the low toneme, written /`/ or B. They are 'punctual (level) tonemes' since their pitch stays constant throughout the vowel that carries them. The signs /^/ and /ˇ/ note respectively the combination of tonemes H+B and B+H carried by one vowel phoneme. These combinations are realised as a 'modulated tone' since pitch varies during the production of the vowel.
tn.cite: Dodo-Bounguendza, Eric. 1993. Esquisse phonologique et morphologique du gisira, langue bantoue (B 41) du Gabon. Thèse de doctorat, Université Libre de Bruxelles. Vol. 1 (phonologie, morphonologie).
tn.note: Two level tonemes, high and low, on vowels; HL and LH on one vowel surface as falling and rising; floating tones; no downstep; a separate demarcative accent realised as vowel length.

3018.dq: El grupo acentual, en su forma básica, se define como una unidad acentuada y aislable de una o dos sílabas. (p.106; contrasted with sect. 1, p.102, OCR: 'El grupo fónico en siriano se define como la unidad mínima que lleva entonación; esta unidad se compone de uno o más grupos acentuales y por lo general se da entre pausas.')
3018.dloc: sect. 2 'El grupo acentual', p.106; sect. 1 'El grupo fónico', p.102 (scan)
3018.prule: Pitch-accent ('tono-acentual') analysis: accent is realised as high tone, unaccented syllables as low tone. The basic accent group (root) is 'S (monosyllable, accented) or S'S (disyllable, low-high, accented on the 2nd syllable). Added syllables (suffixes) are high/accented or low according to a lexical root category (first category: high patterns (a)-(d); second category: all suffixes low). Where two or more accented syllables occur, the main 'acento doble' is predictable: on the first accented syllable if the group ends accented, on the last accented syllable (the one before the final unaccented syllable) if the group ends unaccented. No fixed, quantity-insensitive word-edge position.
3018.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress. Besides the main accent ('acento doble', see Primary), every other high-toned syllable of the accent group is accented (single accent mark), so a word may carry two or more contiguous accents, e.g. [ndò"á'bú'gɨ́] /do'a'bu'gɨ/ 'para sentarse'; which suffix syllables are accented is fixed by the root's lexical category and the suffix pattern (first category patterns (a)-(d); second category: all suffixes low, e.g. /bi'rabugɨ/ 'para jugar'), not by position or alternation.

[p.111] Los grupos acentuales básicos se dividen en dos categorías, de acuerdo a los patrones tono-acentuales que llevan las unidades adicionales. ... Nótese el ace…

3018.tone: The authors never call Siriano a tone language; their frame is accentual with tone derived from accent ('patrones tono-acentuales'): 'El grupo acentual tiene dos niveles tonales determinados por el acento: el tono alto siempre aparece en sílaba acentuada y el tono bajo en sílaba inacentuada' (p.106); fn.2 p.103 (scan) 'La sílaba acentuada siempre lleva tono alto y la inacentuada tono bajo descontando las modificaciones por entonación que producen tono medio.' Several contiguous accented (high) syllables are permitted in one accent group (patterns (b)-(d), p.111), and whether suffix syllables are high or low is a lexical property of the root (first vs second category), so the system is a pitch-accent / privative-tone system rather than a stress rule. Consistent with Barnes 1999 (Amazonian Languages p.212, in the copy consulted): Tucanoan languages 'have accent, or pitch-accent systems', Siriano among those that 'may have two or more contiguous high-pitched syllables, all of these syllables being equally accented'. SAPHON codes 'Suprasegmental: Tone' from Criswell & Brandrup 2000 (not seen).

3021.prule: fixed-initial: primary stress on the first syllable of the word, regardless of syllable weight (Miestamo 2011: 116, citing Korhonen et al. 1973: 23–24); corroborated by Feist 2015: 41, where words consist of stress groups beginning with a stressed syllable and 'odd syllables are stressed'.
3021.srule: Secondary stress falls on the first vowel (V1) of every non-initial foot: weak when that foot is short (allegro), strong when it is long (largo); the second vowel (V2) of a foot is never stressed. Feet are trochaic and at most disyllabic but may consist of V1 alone, so the positions follow the word's foot division (marked | or ' in the dictionary orthography), not a syllable count, and two stressed syllables can be adjacent (tuõdd|ra 'fell.ILL', main|steʹped 'tell.PRS.2PL'). Earlier characterization: secondary stresses present but 'no clear foot type' (Miestamo 2011: 116, relaying Korhonen et al. 1973 and Korhonen 1975).

3022.prule: Stress (tekanan), pitch and duration are said to exist but none is distinctive; the language has no suprasegmental phonemes. tn.quote: La hauteur mélodique a une fonction distinctive en sso, comme dans la quasi-totalité des langues bantoues. Il y a deux registres, haut et bas, ainsi que deux tons distinctifs, le ton haut (noté /H/) et le ton bas (noté /B/). Le caractère contrastif de ces deux tons est exemplifié par les paires minimales présentées en (83). ... Ces deux tons distinctifs peuvent se combiner pour former des tons modulés sur le plan phonétique. Ces derniers ne sont donc pas des tonèmes de la langue mais des réalisations tonales dérivées de tons distinctifs simples.
tn.translation: Pitch has a distinctive function in Sso, as in almost all Bantu languages. There are two registers, high and low, as well as two distinctive tones, the high tone (noted /H/) and the low tone (noted /B/). The contrastive character of these two tones is exemplified by the minimal pairs presented in (83). ... These two distinctive tones can combine to form contour tones on the phonetic level. The latter are therefore not tonemes of the language but tonal realisations derived from simple distinctive tones.

3030.prule: Dynamic (force) stress, usually on the last syllable of the word (p. 178: 'Ударение силовое, обычно приходится на конец слова'). Grammatical suffixes/enclitics (indefinite article -ī, ezafe -e, subject-object marker -ā, pronominal enclitics) are unstressed, so stress stays on the final syllable of the stem. Verb forms are morphologically governed: stress falls on the verbal prefixes (imperative be-/bä-, p. 186 bé-ku, bä́-kun) and on the negative particle nä-/ni-/mä- (nä́-andä, už-nä́-giri), and in past tenses may fall on the stem.
3030.srule: Only in compounds: a secondary stress arises on the first member of compound words (dàst-xålī́ 'empty-handed', main stress word-final); no secondary stress described for non-compound words (Kerimova 1997: 178).

3034.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the (fully suffixed) word, assigned by an iterative right-to-left Main Stress Rule that stops before any 'unstressable' unit (word boundary; the negative suffix -ma-, past -di-, question mi); syllable weight plays no role; loanwords are nativized to the same final stress.
3034.srule: Secondary stress only by demotion (SPE convention): when an unstressable, pre-stressing suffix (negative -ma-, past -di-, question mi) makes the iterative right-to-left Main Stress Rule reapply, the new leftward stress is primary and each earlier-assigned stress -- the word-final syllable and any syllable before a further unstressable suffix -- is weakened by one degree: alɨ́šmadɨlàr 'they were not kindled'; gǽlmæmìšdilæ̀r 'they had not come' (1 on gæl, 2 on miš, 3 on lær). Words without such suffixes carry a single final stress (alɨšdɨlár); no rhythmic secondary stress is described.

tn.quote: Vowel length is absent in Island Kiwai, though frequent in Wabuda and also encountered in the northern languages. The suprasegmental features manifest themselves in a complex stress system with rhythm patterns, and a two-tone system. 3041.prule: No rule of stress position is given. Trager analyses Isleta and Sandía (jointly with Taos and Picurís) as having three degrees of stress, loud (main), medial (secondary) and weak, with loud and medial stresses cross-classified by three tones (normal, low, high); vowels are long under loud or medial stress and short/obscured under weak stress. Stress and tone are written lexically on every listed word; loud stress falls on different syllables in different Isleta nouns (pˌapˈade, tˌutˈude: loud on the 2nd syllable; cˈunu, mˈatuʔude, łˈulide: loud on the 1st; ʔupˌiwʔˈude: loud on the 3rd, and ʔùʔˈide, pʻiwʔˈide: normal loud stress on the 2nd) and one noun is recorded with two placements (ʔə̀wˈade ~ ʔˈəw-). The only placement statement in the source is tone-conditioned relative loudness: among non-normal tones the first of two lows or two highs is loud, and a high outranks a low. The source never states that stress is free, contrastive or unpredictable, so the verdict is the tone system with no stress rule.
3041.srule: Exists; placement not stated. Trager sets up a 'medial (secondary)' stress degree beside loud (main) and weak stress, marked with a lowered stroke and written per word (Isleta pˌapˈade, tˌutˈude, kˌecˈude, mˌatˈunan, ʔupˌiwʔˈude, p. 567; Sandia pˌapˈajde, tˌutˈujde, p. 566); vowels are long under medial as under loud stress. No rule locates medial stress in the word; the only general statement ranks co-occurring high/low-toned stressed syllables: 'of two lows or two highs the first is loud, of a high and a low together the high is loud'.
